title: What they said at the time

clips.q: Why did it happen so quickly? And why were they not in tune with it while it was building?
clips.who: **Richard P. Simon**, analyst at Goldman, Sachs, in The New York Times, Dec 19, 1982[^1]

clips.q: We have been erratic, unbelievable, and we have said things we didn’t mean. That has to come to an end.
clips.who: **James J. Morgan**, Atari chief executive, January 1984, as quoted in The New York Times[^7]

clips.q: Warner essentially gave away the company, in hopes Tramiel could make something happen.
clips.who: **Lee Isgur**, analyst at Paine Webber, in The New York Times, Jul 3, 1984[^7]

clips.q: It’s clear that the old Atari was dead. It just wasn’t worth anything.
clips.who: **David Lawrence**, analyst at Montgomery Securities, in The New York Times, Jul 3, 1984[^7]

clips.q: That has to be the greatest acquisition in history.
clips.who: **Donald Valentine**, early Atari backer, on Warner’s $28 million purchase, in The New York Times, Dec 19, 1982[^1]

clips.q: 8 years ago, when I came back, the brand was given for dead.
clips.who: **Frédéric Chesnais**, outgoing chief executive of Atari SA, April 2021[^20]
